feedback.problem: What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{(2{n}^{2}+1)(2{n}^{2}-1)}{3{n}^{4}(1-n)}$ for $n\ge 2?$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we multiply out the numerator and denominator of the sequence and get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{(2{n}^{2}+1)(2{n}^{2}-1)}{3{n}^{4}(1-n)}=\frac{4{n}^{4}-1}{3{n}^{4}-3{n}^{5}}.
$$

So to find the limit, we will need to compute

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{4{n}^{4}-1}{3{n}^{4}-3{n}^{5}}.
$$

The dominant term in the denominator is $-3{n}^{5},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{5}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{4{n}^{4}-1}{3{n}^{4}-3{n}^{5}} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{4{n}^{4}}{{n}^{5}}-\frac{1}{{n}^{5}})}{(\frac{3{n}^{4}}{{n}^{5}}-\frac{3{n}^{5}}{{n}^{5}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{4}{n}-\frac{1}{{n}^{5}})}{(\frac{3}{n}-3)} \\  & =\frac{0-0}{0-3} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the sequence converges and its limit is $0.$
